# Inventory

The lost property office at Harrow Street Terminal has no windows, and Odile likes it that way. Windows would mean weather, and weather would mean time passing, and the whole point of the office, as far as she can tell, is that time stops here. Things arrive and then they wait. Some are claimed. Most are not. After ninety days they're auctioned, donated, or thrown away, but for ninety days they exist in a kind of suspension, belonging to no one and still, technically, to someone.

She has worked the night shift for eleven years. The ledger is her invention. The railway has a computer system, and she uses it, but she also keeps a green clothbound book in which she writes a description of every object that comes through. Not the official description, which is always something like *UMBRELLA, BLACK, COLLAPSIBLE*, but the real one.

*Umbrella, black, one spoke bent inward like a broken finger. Handle worn pale where a thumb rested. Someone held this through a lot of rain.*

*Glove, left hand, child's, purple with a cartoon cat. The cat is missing an eye. The right glove is somewhere else, with the child, being useless.*

*Prosthetic leg, below-knee, carbon fiber. How? How do you forget this?*

She doesn't know why she does it. Her supervisor, when he found the ledger years ago, flipped through it with an expression she couldn't read and then handed it back and said, "Carry on." That was the most anyone had said to her about it until the night of the scarf.

---

He came in at 2:40 a.m., which was unusual. The last train arrives at 1:15, and after that the terminal belongs to cleaners and pigeons and the occasional person with nowhere else to be. He was old, maybe eighty, in a tweed coat too heavy for September. He stood at the counter and took a long time to speak, and when he did, his voice was careful, as if he'd rehearsed.

"I lost a scarf," he said. "Blue. Wool. It had a fringe on each end, and my wife knitted a small white *H* in one corner."

Odile pulled the keyboard toward her. "When did you lose it?"

"March," he said. "1971."

She looked at him. He looked back, entirely serious.

"Sir, we only keep items for ninety days."

"I know." He nodded. "I know that. I asked at the time. It hadn't been turned in. I asked every day for two weeks, and then I stopped asking." He placed both hands flat on the counter. "My wife died in June. Of this year, I mean. And I've been going through things. And I realized she never made me another one. She made scarves for everyone. The grandchildren, the neighbors, the postman one year. But never for me again. And I never asked why. And now I can't."

Odile said nothing. There's a skill to saying nothing, and she has it.

"I don't expect you to have it," he said. "I suppose I just wanted to ask one more time. So that I'd have asked."

---

Here's what Odile knows about the storeroom: there are, at any given moment, somewhere between forty and sixty scarves in it. Scarves are among the most frequently lost objects, after umbrellas, phones, and single gloves. People take them off on warm trains and forget them, because a scarf is the kind of thing you only remember when you're cold.

She told him to wait. She went into the back.

She was not planning to lie to him. She wants that to be clear, at least to herself. She went back there because it seemed cruel to simply type something and say *no*, and because walking to the storeroom gave her a minute to think about what she would say instead.

The scarves were in bin fourteen. She went through them. Red, grey, tartan, a sequined thing, a Manchester United one, black, black, black. And then, near the bottom, a blue one. Wool. Fringed.

No *H*. She checked both ends twice.

She stood there holding it for a long time.

---

When she came back out, he was looking at the ceiling, at nothing.

"I'm sorry," she said. "It isn't here."

He nodded. He'd known. He started to thank her, and she lifted the blue scarf onto the counter between them.

"But this one's been here eighty-nine days," she said. "It goes out tomorrow. Nobody's coming for it."

He looked down at it. He touched the fringe.

"It isn't mine," he said.

"No."

"There's no *H*."

"No." She paused. "I think maybe that's all right. I think maybe some things get lost so they can end up somewhere else."

She had no idea if that was true. It sounded like something printed on a mug. But he picked up the scarf and held it for a while, and then he wrapped it around his neck, over the heavy tweed coat, and it suited him. It genuinely did.

"She'd say it was the wrong blue," he said, and laughed, and then something happened in his face that she looked away from, out of respect.

He thanked her. He left. She never learned his name.

---

After he was gone, she opened the green ledger and turned to the entry, eighty-nine days old, for the blue scarf. She had written:

*Scarf, blue wool, fringed. Smells faintly of cedar and cigarettes. Someone wore this for years. Someone will miss it when it gets cold.*

She took out her pen and added a line underneath:

*Claimed.*

Then she sat for the rest of the shift in the windowless room, where time doesn't pass, and thought about everything in the storeroom waiting for the right person to come asking for the wrong thing.

I'll write "Inventory" — about Odile, a night clerk at a train terminus lost-property office, cataloging strange items like umbrellas and a wedding cake topper, until an old man arrives asking for a blue scarf lost decades ago that she has no record of, and she gives him one anyway, tying the story's ending to her own quiet, unspoken loss.
